summary:
Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex sexual activity. No sodomy statute was inherited from the French protectorate period, which began in 1867, or enacted after independence in 1953, and the age of consent is 15 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Legislation contains no non-discrimination provisions on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Trans visitors have no route to legal recognition. Cambodian law does not permit changes to gender markers on official documents, and gender-affirming surgery is not legally available.

Official posture is cooperative on paper. At the 2019 Universal Periodic Review Cambodia accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage, and at the 2024 review it accepted all 12 recommendations on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, seven of them on marriage equality, alongside legal gender recognition based on self-defined identity and anti-discrimination measures. A civil-society joint submission was filed in December 2023.

That posture has not been matched by statutory protection. In 2015 a Council of Ministers spokesman claimed existing law already protected LGBT people, a claim the Cambodian Center for Human Rights disputed. The same year the Ministry of Information wrote to media outlets asking them to stop mocking the LGBT community, citing the Constitution's protection of LGBT honour and rights. In February 2011 tourism businesses launched the 'Adore Cambodia!' campaign to signal welcome to LGBT tourists, which the Ministry of Tourism endorsed, saying it had no policy to discriminate and supported them.

Enforcement and street-level violence are the principal risk. A Cambodian Centre for Human Rights study documented more than 135 cases of harassment and abuse against transgender women on city streets, and recorded a Siem Reap police practice of targeting transgender sex workers and forcing them to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water; transgender sex workers there were also made to leave the area, sometimes after being forced to bathe naked, while cisgender sex workers were not documented as receiving the same treatment. A 2016 CCHR report found about 38% of surveyed transgender women had been arrested, with over 90% of those saying the arrest was because they were transgender. The 2017 US State Department human rights report listed violence against LGBTI persons among Cambodia's most significant human rights issues, noting frequent harassment and bullying over appearance and over work in the entertainment and commercial sex sectors, with more than 100 incidents of violence or abuse reported by a local LGBTI organisation. The same report found no official discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, citizenship, education or health care.

In custody, the Cambodian Human Rights Committee president Keo Remy said in February 2025 that transgender prisoners who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from Correctional Centre 1, the men's facility, to Correctional Centre 2, the women's facility at Prey Sar. The statement was made in praise of the centre rather than as a published regulation, and no statute or formal policy text is cited.

Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have a visible LGBT scene with bars and clubs, and Pride parades have run annually since 2003, with the first Siem Reap Pride in 2018.
tangentialFactors:
The UN Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has visited Cambodia and issued a report identifying good practices and remaining challenges and recommending stronger protection; an unofficial Khmer translation was prepared for national stakeholders.

A 2014 UNDP and USAID country report reviewed the legal and social environment for LGBT people and civil society, drawing on a national LGBT community dialogue held in Phnom Penh in January 2013, participant conversations, an NGO and community-based organisation survey, and a desk review of published literature.

In January 2019 Cambodia received UN recommendations from Iceland, Mexico, Sweden and Uruguay to establish educational programmes and campaigns raising awareness of LGBT people and discrimination.

The 2017 US State Department report also noted increased government restrictions on speech, assembly and press freedom, a constraint on civic space that affects LGBT organising alongside other groups.

A 2010 report described a concentration of poor and working-class LGBT people in Beoung Kak 2 in Phnom Penh, then described as the country's first gay town.
localsOnly:
Family rejection is documented as widespread. A Rainbow Community Kampuchea study reported in 2019 found 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 had suffered emotional abuse by a family member, and 35% of under-35 participants had considered suicide because of family rejection. The study documented a 27-year-old transgender man forced by his mother into rehabilitation to 'fix his gender'.

Schools are a documented site of abuse. Many LGBT Cambodians report bullying at school. In June 2017 the government announced life-skills courses covering sexual health, gender-based violence, gender identity and combating discrimination against the LGBT population; these became part of the curriculum in all Cambodian schools in 2018. Before the rollout, LGBT activists working with the Ministry of Education trained more than 3,000 teachers in 20 schools across nine Cambodian provinces.

Health access is a concern for residents. In 2019 the director of the Cambodia Human Rights Committee reported rising HIV infections within the LGBT community, especially among people under 30.
outOfScopeNotes:
The February 2025 statement on transferring transgender prisoners between Correctional Centre 1 and Correctional Centre 2 is not a published regulation and no statute or formal policy text has been identified; how it is applied in practice is unresolved.

The 2015 claim by a Council of Ministers spokesman that existing law already protected LGBT people was disputed by the Cambodian Center for Human Rights, and no provision has been identified that gives it effect.

The 2024 Universal Periodic Review acceptances, including on marriage equality and legal gender recognition, have not been matched by enacted legislation in the sources reviewed.

Documented case counts, including the 135 or more cases recorded by the Cambodian Centre for Human Rights and the more than 100 incidents reported by a local LGBTI organisation in 2017, are monitoring figures rather than population rates; they record what was reported to those organisations and do not establish prevalence. The 2016 finding that about 38% of surveyed transgender women had been arrested rests on a survey sample whose sampling frame is not stated in the sources reviewed.
